beats.say: A free Hershey's Kiss outsells a priced Lindt truffle.
A simple chocolate kiss, no frills.
The same two sweets, but the kiss costs nothing.
When the kiss is free, 69% take it, despite a 14-cent gap. Sounds generous.
But it stops comparison; free wins.
The free kiss removes any price reference, so the remaining 14-cent difference feels irrelevant.
Consequently, 69% pick the free kiss while only 31% still buy the truffle.
A 73% preference for the truffle evaporates once the kiss is free.
You see it everywhere: a bakery offers a chocolate croissant for $2.50, a plain croissant for $2.00, and a free coffee.
The free coffee makes the croissant feel like the smart buy.
A gym lists a month pass $30, a day pass $5, and a free trial week; the free trial pushes the month pass.
If something is free, expect it to dominate choices. Follow for more.
